# Events that trigger workflows

You can configure your workflows to run when specific activity on GitHub happens, at a scheduled time, or when an event outside of GitHub occurs.

Copy markdown

## In this article

## About events that trigger workflows

Workflow triggers are events that cause a workflow to run. For more information about how to use workflow triggers, see [Triggering a workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow).

Some events have multiple activity types. For these events, you can specify which activity types will trigger a workflow run. For more information about what each activity type means, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads).

Note

 Not all webhook events trigger workflows.

Like GitHub Actions workflows, agentic workflows can be triggered by repository events and schedules. For an example, see [Creating GitHub Agentic Workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/github-agentic-workflows/creating-github-agentic-workflows).

## `branch_protection_rule`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`branch_protection_rule`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#branch_protection_rule) | - `created` - `edited` - `deleted` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#branch_protection_rule). By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.

Runs your workflow when branch protection rules in the workflow repository are changed. For more information about branch protection rules, see [About protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches). For information about the branch protection rule APIs, see [Branches](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/branches#object-branchprotectionrule) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for branches and their settings](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/branches).

For example, you can run a workflow when a branch protection rule has been `created` or `deleted`:

```yaml
on:
  branch_protection_rule:
    types: [created, deleted]
```

## `check_run`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`check_run`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_run) | - `created` - `rerequested` - `completed` - `requested_action` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_run). By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- To prevent recursive workflows, this event does not trigger workflows if the check run's check suite was created by GitHub Actions or if the check suite's head SHA is associated with GitHub Actions.

Runs your workflow when activity related to a check run occurs. A check run is an individual test that is part of a check suite. For information, see [Using the REST API to interact with checks](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/using-the-rest-api-to-interact-with-checks). For information about the check run APIs, see [Checks](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/checks#object-checkrun) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for check runs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs).

For example, you can run a workflow when a check run has been `rerequested` or `completed`.

```yaml
on:
  check_run:
    types: [rerequested, completed]
```

## `check_suite`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`check_suite`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_suite) | - `completed` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_suite). Although only the `completed` activity type is supported, specifying the activity type will keep your workflow specific if more activity types are added in the future. By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- To prevent recursive workflows, this event does not trigger workflows if the check suite was created by GitHub Actions or if the check suite's head SHA is associated with GitHub Actions.

Runs your workflow when check suite activity occurs. A check suite is a collection of the check runs created for a specific commit. Check suites summarize the status and conclusion of the check runs that are in the suite. For information, see [Using the REST API to interact with checks](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/using-the-rest-api-to-interact-with-checks). For information about the check suite APIs, see [Checks](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/checks#object-checksuite) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for check suites](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/suites).

For example, you can run a workflow when a check suite has been `completed`.

```yaml
on:
  check_suite:
    types: [completed]
```

## `create`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`create`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#create) | Not applicable | Last commit on the created branch or tag | Branch or tag created |

Note

 An event will not be created when you create more than three tags at once.

Runs your workflow when someone creates a Git reference (Git branch or tag) in the workflow's repository. For information about the APIs to create a Git reference, see [Git](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/git#mutation-createref) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for Git references](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/refs#create-a-reference).

For example, you can run a workflow when the `create` event occurs.

```yaml
on:
  create
```

## `delete`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`delete`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#delete) | Not applicable | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- An event will not be created when you delete more than three tags at once.

blocks.text:
a conditional with the github.event.workflow_run.conclusion property. For example, this workflow will run whenever a workflow named "Build" completes, but the on-success job will only run if the "Build" workflow succeeded, and the on-failure job will only run if the "Build" workflow failed: 
 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Build ]
 types: [ completed ]

 jobs: 
 on-success: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' }} 
 steps: 
 - run: echo 'The triggering workflow passed' 
 on-failure: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'failure' }} 
 steps: 
 - run: echo 'The triggering workflow failed' 
 
 Limiting your workflow to run based on branches 
 You can use the branches or branches-ignore filter to specify what branches the triggering workflow must run on in order to trigger your workflow. For more information, see Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions . For example, a workflow with the following trigger will only run when the workflow named Build runs on a branch named canary . 
 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Build ]
 types: [ requested ]
 branches: [ canary ]
 
 Using data from the triggering workflow 
 You can access the workflow_run event payload that corresponds to the workflow that triggered your workflow. For example, if your triggering workflow generates artifacts, a workflow triggered with the workflow_run event can access these artifacts. 
 The following workflow uploads data as an artifact. (In this simplified example, the data is the pull request number.) 
 name: Upload data 

 on: 
 pull_request: 

 jobs: 
 upload: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 

 steps: 
 - name: Save PR number 
 env: 
 PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.number }} 
 run: |
 mkdir -p ./pr
 echo $PR_NUMBER > ./pr/pr_number
 - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 
 with: 
 name: pr_number 
 path: pr/ 
 
 When a run of the above workflow completes, it triggers a run of the following workflow. The following workflow uses the github.event.workflow_run context and the actions/download-artifact@v5 action to download the artifact that was uploaded by the above workflow, then comments on the pull request whose number was uploaded as an artifact. 
 name: Use the data 

 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Upload data ]
 types: 
 - completed 

 jobs: 
 download: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 permissions: 
 actions: read 
 issues: write 
 steps: 
 - name: 'Download artifact' 
 uses: actions/download-artifact@v5 
 with: 
 name: pr_number 
 # do not extract in the workspace dir that may contain executable scripts 
 path: ${{ runner.temp }}/artifacts 
 run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }} 
 github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} 

 - name: 'Comment on PR' 
 uses: actions/github-script@v8 
 with: 
 github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} 
 script: |
 const fs = require('fs');
 const path = require('path');
 const temp = '${{ runner.temp }}/artifacts';
 const issue_number_raw = fs.readFileSync(path.join(temp, 'pr_number'), 'utf8').trim();
 const issue_number = Number(issue_number_raw);
 if (!Number.isInteger(issue_number)) {
 throw new Error(`Invalid PR number in pr_number artifact: "${issue_number_raw}"`);
 }
 await github.rest.issues.createComment({
 owner: context.repo.owner,
 repo: context.repo.repo,
 issue_number: issue_number,
 body: 'Thank you for the PR!'
 });

{"content":"# gh-867 — RCA

## Root Cause Analysis

**Bug**: PRs merged by the Machine Merge Bot land on `main` but never trigger an 'Agent Pack Release' run — releases stall until an operator manually dispatches one (live 2026-10-11/12: #863 22:01Z, #866 00:11Z, both rescued by manual dispatch runs 38179243031 / 38188359001).

**Root cause**: `.github/workflows/agent-pack-release.yml` reacts to new commits on `main` ONLY through its `push` trigger. GitHub suppresses workflow triggers for events authored with `GITHUB_TOKEN` (documented: "events triggered by the GITHUB_TOKEN will not create a new workflow run"), and the merge bot's merge push lands with `GITHUB_TOKEN` — so the merge commit reaches `main` without any push event and the release workflow never learns about it. Human/operator merges (PAT/app-token pushes) fire normally — exactly the 21:14–21:18Z contrast pair in the ticket.

**Impact**: every machine-merged agent-code PR is invisible to the release pipeline. The SM fleet resolves agent packs via the 'latest' release knob, so machine-landed fixes never ship — tonight this twice stalled the fa #1457 fix pipeline until an operator noticed.

**Why the gh-844 kicker (previous mitigation) is insufficient**: the release kicker (`agent-pack-release-kicker.yml`, gh-844) is a 10-minute polling *belt*, not a trigger — it cannot meet the ~2-minute acceptance, and in both gh-867 incidents no release run appeared until a human dispatched one, i.e. the belt demonstrably did not rescue the machine-merge window either. The structural gap remains: nothing reacts *event-driven* to the machine merge completing.

**Fix approach** (ticket option 3): add a `workflow_run` trigger on 'Machine Merge Bot' completions to `agent-pack-release.yml`. The bot's own run completion is a normal GitHub event (workflow_run chains up to 3 levels are allowed — `Agent Docs → Machine Merge Bot → Agent Pack Release` is 2), so a machine merge now cuts a release within seconds. Two deliberate design points:
- **No `branches:` filter on the trigger** — the bot's `workflow_run.head_branch` is the *PR branch*, never `main`; a `branches: [main]` filter would silence the trigger entirely. "Filtered to main" is realized by the existing tag…main diff + `dist/.no-release` no-op (same dedup as the kicker's double-dispatch, gh-690).
- **Job gate on `conclusion == 'success'`** — the bot completes on every label latch tick (merging nothing) and `completed` covers failures; only a successful bot run may cut a release.
- The "Sync to current main" step (gh-690) is extended from push-only to push + workflow_run so a queued run releases current main; manual dispatch stays ref-targeted.
- Push trigger and kicker stay untouched (belt AND suspenders); the concurrency group + no-release no-op absorb double dispatches.

**Previous attempt**: gh-844 added the 10-minute release kicker after the 2026-10-10 #841 incident. It mitigates dropped push events generically but is polling-based: it misses the ~2-minute AC and, per both gh-867 incidents, did not rescue the machine-merge window (manual dispatch was still required).

OK. Now let me write the RCA and design.

## Root Cause Analysis

**Bug**: PRs merged by the Machine Merge Bot produce no 'Agent Pack Release' run; releases stall until an operator manually dispatches.

**Root cause**: The release workflow's only automatic trigger reacting to "new commits on main" is the `push` trigger. GitHub suppresses workflow triggers on pushes authored with `GITHUB_TOKEN` (to prevent recursive workflow loops) — the merge bot's merge push lands with GITHUB_TOKEN, so no push event fires. The gh-844 kicker (10-min polling belt) is the only fallback, and per the ticket it failed to rescue both incidents (merge → manual dispatch; >15 min gaps) — its schedule-based polling is both slower than the AC (~2 min) and evidently not firing in the machine-merge window.

Wait, I should be careful: can I honestly claim the kicker "failed"? The ticket evidence: manual dispatch runs exist. I can't verify kicker logs. I'll state the RCA as: the only *reliable, event-driven* trigger plane is suppressed for the machine merge path; the scheduled kicker either lagged or didn't fire, and in both incidents the release required a human dispatch. The structural fix is to make the machine merge completion itself an event-driven trigger for the release (ticket option 3).

Hmm — actually, let me reconsider whether I should also make the kicker... no, minimum targeted fix: add workflow_run trigger. 

Now the design details:

### agent-pack-release.yml changes

1. Add trigger:
```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths-ignore: ...
  workflow_run:
    # gh-867: the merge bot's GITHUB_TOKEN push never fires the push trigger
    # above (GitHub suppresses workflow triggers on GITHUB_TOKEN pushes).
    # The bot's own COMPLETION is a normal event though — so the release
    # fires seconds after a machine merge instead of waiting on the 10-min
    # kicker belt (or an operator).
    workflows: ['Machine Merge Bot']
    types: [completed]
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs: ...
```

2. Job gate — the workflow_run fires on EVERY bot completion (the bot runs on label events even when it merges nothing), and `completed` covers failures. Gate:
```yaml
jobs:
  release:
    if: >-
      github.event_name != 'workflow_run' ||
      github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success'
```
Failed bot runs (no merge happened) must not cut a release; successful ones let the base-tag...main diff decide (docs-only/empty merges no-op via dist/.no-release, same dedup as the kicker's double-dispatch).

Hmm wait — should the gate be on the job or each step? Job-level `if` is cleaner. But careful: job-level `if` with `always()`? No, default status check is fine (no needs).

3. "Sync to current main" step gate: currently `if: github.event_name == 'push'`. For workflow_run events, GITHUB_SHA is... For workflow_run, `github.sha` is the default branch's... Let me be precise. Per GitHub docs (events that trigger workflows → `workflow_run`): `GITHUB_SHA` = "Last commit on the default branch" — hmm, I actually need to double check this. There was a change: originally workflow_run checkout defaulted to the default branch. Yes: for `workflow_run`, the ref/sha default is the **default branch** (main), not the triggering run's head. Hmm, actually I recall that `actions/checkout` on workflow_run checks out the commit of the DEFAULT branch... but there are many blog posts noting that for workflow_run, `github.sha` is the sha of the default branch's latest commit. Either way, syncing to origin/main is the safe move — the merge may have landed after the workflow_run event was generated. Extend the gate:

```yaml
if: github.event_name == 'push' || github.event_name == 'workflow_run'
```

But the comment says "Gated to push events — a manual dispatch may deliberately target a non-main ref." Keep dispatch excluded.

4. IMPORTANT — the "Bump versions.json" ledger step pushes directly to main. With the workflow_run path now firing the release, after a machine merge the release runs: build (bumps versions.json), ledger push to main with PUSH_TOKEN (SOURCE_GITHUB_TOKEN || GITHUB_TOKEN)... wait, that push to main — does IT re-trigger the push trigger? If PUSH_TOKEN is the ai-teammate app token → push event fires → push-triggered release run → next run no-ops. That's the existing behavior for push-triggered releases too (the ledger push already happens there — and the old comment said squash merge carried [skip ci] to avoid re-trigger; the direct push path... hmm, `chore(release): bump agent versions` has no [skip ci], so a push-triggered release's ledger push re-triggers the release workflow, which then no-ops via empty diff. That already exists today; my change doesn't alter it. Also the workflow_run-triggered release's ledger push with GITHUB_TOKEN (if SOURCE_GITHUB_TOKEN unset) is suppressed — consistent.

5. Guard against the workflow_run loop: workflow_run triggers do NOT chain — a workflow_run trigger fires only from workflows that are NOT themselves triggered by workflow_run? Actually: " workflows triggered by the workflow_run event... cannot trigger another workflow run via workflow_run"? The rule: to prevent recursive runs, GitHub does not trigger a workflow_run when the upstream workflow was itself triggered by another workflow_run completion... Precisely: "you can't use workflow_run to trigger another workflow_run in an infinite chain; a workflow_run event will not trigger workflows that would create recursion". Actually the documented restriction: a workflow triggered by `workflow_run` will NOT trigger `workflow_run` listeners?? Hmm. The actual rule (docs): "This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file is on the default branch." And about recursion: GitHub prevents recursive workflow_run chains — a workflow_run-triggered run completing does NOT fire workflow_run triggers. But the MACHINE MERGE BOT is triggered by pull_request/check_run/workflow_run(Agent Docs!)... wait, machine-merge.yml has `workflow_run: workflows: ['Agent Docs']`. So the merge bot is itself triggered by a workflow_run event! Does its completion fire OUR new workflow_run trigger? 

The recursion guard: GitHub docs state — "workflows triggered by a workflow_run event... will not trigger another workflow's workflow_run"? Let me recall precisely. From GitHub docs (Events that trigger workflows → workflow_run):

"Note: You can't use workflow_run to trigger a workflow run from another workflow_run... To prevent recursive workflow runs, a workflow_run event will not be triggered by a workflow that was triggered by another workflow_run event." 

Hmm — I believe the documented behavior is: **workflow runs triggered by the `workflow_run` event cannot trigger another `workflow_run`** — no wait. Let me think about what's documented: In "Events that trigger workflows", under workflow_run: "The workflow_run event... will not run for workflow runs triggered by another workflow_run event." Hmm, I genuinely recall something like: "A workflow run triggered by a workflow_run event cannot trigger another workflow_run event" — that's the anti-recursion rule. 

The MERGE BOT is triggered by workflow_run('Agent Docs') — its runs ARE workflow_run-triggered. If the anti-recursion rule blocks workflow_run chains, then our release workflow_run trigger on 'Machine Merge Bot' would NEVER fire!! That would make option 3 useless — which might be exactly why the incident recurred... no wait, the kicker was the gh-844 fix; option 3 was never implemented.

Let me get this fact right. GitHub docs (as of 2023+): under `workflow_run`:

> "The workflow_run event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file is on the default branch. ... You can't use `workflow_run` to chain workflow runs that would create a recursive loop. A workflow triggered by `workflow_run` will not trigger another `workflow_run` when it completes."

Hmm, I actually now recall the precise documented limitation from the GitHub docs troubleshooting: "A workflow can't trigger another workflow run when using GITHUB_TOKEN" (push suppression), AND for workflow_run specifically: **"Note: The workflow_run event will not trigger a new workflow run for work…

# Machine SM — thin stub over the FROZEN machine loop
# (IstiN/dmtools-agentic-workflows, reusable).
#
# Same freeze contract as dmtools-dart's machine-sm.yml: the workflow is
# pinned to an immutable SHA; agent code and the dmtools CLI resolve from
# RELEASES at run time via this repo's variables:
#   vars.AGENTS_VERSION  — dmtools-agents release tag ('latest' default)
#   vars.DMTOOLS_VERSION — dmtools-dart CLI release tag ('latest' default)
# Bump a version = repo-settings edit, never a workflow edit.
# NO caller-side concurrency: the factory owns the `machine-sm` group.

name: 'Machine SM'

run-name: >-
  🧹 SM ${{
    github.event_name == 'workflow_dispatch' && 'manual tick' ||
    format('tick {0}', github.event.schedule || '') }}${{
  github.event.inputs.dryRun == 'true' && ' (dry)' || '' }}

on:
  schedule:
    - cron: '*/10 * * * *'   # short ticks — the engine idles when busy
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      dryRun:
        description: 'Log the plan, perform no action'
        required: false
        type: boolean
        default: true

permissions:
  contents: write         # checkout + silent update-branch pushes
  issues: write           # labels + close-issue safety net
  pull-requests: write    # update-branch + merge
  checks: write           # bridge-free validation stamps
  actions: write          # workflow_dispatch on the teammate workflow

jobs:
  sm:
    # Pinned to the immutable SHA of IstiN/dmtools-agentic-workflows main
    # (the frozen machine-loop home; bump the SHA only together with the
    # matching loop change).
    uses: IstiN/dmtools-agentic-workflows/.github/workflows/factory-sm.yml@main
    with:
      # No .dmtools/config.js in this repo — the machine logins ride the
      # deployment-level input (#687, gh-728), exactly like the factory's
      # contract. Comma-separated LIST: the agent harness bot AND the CI
      # bot — github-actions[bot] authors its own PRs (live fa PR #1249)
      # and must ride the machine path (owner directive 2026-10-05).
      machine-author: 'ai-teammate,github-actions[bot]'
      # This repo dispatches no CI on PR heads (docs checks only) — the SM
      # leaves validation to the event-driven merge bot and labels.
      ci-workflow: ''
      # Manual ticks default to dry; cron ticks run live.
      dryRun: ${{ github.event.inputs.dryRun || 'false' }}
      # Factory-state snapshot → factory-data branch (board: site/factory,
      # third tab; fa machine-sm.yml parity — transport lives in
      # js/factoryState.js, publishing is opt-in per factory).
      state-publish: '{"channel":"release","tag":"factory-data","asset":"agents-state.json"}'
      # Silent branch updates: input channel (github.token via secrets/in
      # blocks arrives empty through a reusable call — live-verified).
      silent-token: ${{ github.token }}
    secrets:
      SOURCE_GITHUB_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SOURCE_GITHUB_TOKEN }}
      SILENT_GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SILENT_GH_TOKEN }}

# Triggering a workflow

How to automatically trigger GitHub Actions workflows

Copy markdown

## In this article

## Prerequisites

To learn more about workflows and triggering workflows, see [Workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/workflows).

## Triggering a workflow from a workflow

When you use the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` to perform tasks, events triggered by the `GITHUB_TOKEN` will not create a new workflow run, with the following exceptions:

- `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` events always create workflow runs.
- `pull_request` events with the `opened`, `synchronize`, or `reopened` activity types: when a workflow using `GITHUB_TOKEN` creates or updates a pull request, the resulting `pull_request` event creates workflow runs in an **approval-required** state. The pull request displays a banner in the merge box, and a user with write access to the repository can start the runs by selecting **Approve workflows to run**. Other `pull_request` activity types (such as `labeled`, `edited`, or `closed`) do not create workflow runs. This prevents recursive workflow runs while still allowing CI workflows to run on pull requests created by automation. For more information about approving workflow runs, see [Approving workflow runs from forks](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/approve-runs-from-forks).

For all other events, this behavior prevents you from accidentally creating recursive workflow runs. For example, if a workflow run pushes code using the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a new workflow will not run even when the repository contains a workflow configured to run when `push` events occur. For more information, see [Use GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication in workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/authenticate-with-github_token).

If you do want to trigger a workflow from within a workflow run, you can use a GitHub App installation access token or a personal access token instead of `GITHUB_TOKEN` to trigger events that require a token. Using one of these alternatives also lets `pull_request` workflows run automatically (without the approval prompt described above) when the pull request is created or updated by automation.

If you use a GitHub App, you'll need to create a GitHub App and store the app ID and private key as secrets. For more information, see [Making authenticated API requests with a GitHub App in a GitHub Actions workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/making-authenticated-api-requests-with-a-github-app-in-a-github-actions-workflow). If you use a personal access token, you'll need to create a personal access token and store it as a secret. For more information about creating a personal access token, see [Managing your personal access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens). For more information about storing secrets, see [Using secrets in GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets).

To minimize your GitHub Actions usage costs, ensure that you don't create recursive or unintended workflow runs.

For example, the following workflow uses a personal access token (stored as a secret called `MY_TOKEN`) to add a label to an issue via GitHub CLI. Any workflows that run when a label is added will run once this step is performed.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened

jobs:
  label_issue:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MY_TOKEN }}
          ISSUE_URL: ${{ github.event.issue.html_url }}
        run: |
          gh issue edit $ISSUE_URL --add-label "triage"
```

Conversely, the following workflow uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` to add a label to an issue. It will not trigger any workflows that run when a label is added.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened

jobs:
  label_issue:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          ISSUE_URL: ${{ github.event.issue.html_url }}
        run: |
          gh issue edit $ISSUE_URL --add-label "triage"
```

## Using events to trigger workflows

Use the `on` key to specify what events trigger your workflow. For more information about events you can use, see [Events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows).

### Using a single event

For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when a push is made to any branch in the workflow's repository:

```yaml
on: push
```

### Using multiple events

You can specify a single event or multiple events. For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when a push is made to any branch in the repository or when someone forks the repository:

```yaml
on: [push, fork]
```

If you specify multiple events, only one of those events needs to occur to trigger your workflow. If multiple triggering events for your workflow occur at the same time, multiple workflow runs will be triggered.

### Using activity types and filters with multiple events

You can use activity types and filters to further control when your workflow will run. For more information, see Using event activity types and Using filters. If you specify activity types or filters for an event and your workflow triggers on multiple events, you must configure each event separately. You must append a colon (`:`) to all events, including events without configuration.

For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when:

- A label is created
- A push is made to the `main` branch in the repository
- A push is made to a GitHub Pages-enabled branch

```yaml
on:
  label:
    types:
      - created
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  page_build:
```

## Using event activity types

Some events have activity types that give you more control over when your workflow should run. Use `on.<event_name>.types` to define the type of event activity that will trigger a workflow run.

For example, the `issue_comment` event has the `created`, `edited`, and `deleted` activity types. If your workflow triggers on the `label` event, it will run whenever a label is created, edited, or deleted. If you specify the `created` activity type for the `label` event, your workflow will run when a label is created but not when a label is edited or deleted.

```yaml
on:
  label:
    types:
      - created
```

If you specify multiple activity types, only one of those event activity types needs to occur to trigger your workflow. If multiple triggering event activity types for your workflow occur at the same time, multiple workflow runs will be triggered. For example, the following workflow triggers when an issue is opened or labeled. If an issue with two labels is opened, three workflow runs will start: one for the issue opened event and two for the two issue labeled events.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened
      - labeled
```

For more information about each event and their activity types, see [Events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows).

## Using filters

Some events have filters that give you more control over when your workflow should run.

For example, the `push` event has a `branches` filter that causes your workflow to run only when a push to a branch that matches the `branches` filter occurs, instead of when any push occurs.

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
      - 'releases/**'
```

### Using filters to target specific branches for pull request events

When using the `pull_request` and `pull_request_target` events, you can configure a workflow to run only for pull requests that target specific branches.

# Events that trigger workflows

You can configure your workflows to run when specific activity on GitHub happens, at a scheduled time, or when an event outside of GitHub occurs.

Copy markdown

## In this article

## About events that trigger workflows

Workflow triggers are events that cause a workflow to run. For more information about how to use workflow triggers, see [Triggering a workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow).

Some events have multiple activity types. For these events, you can specify which activity types will trigger a workflow run. For more information about what each activity type means, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads).

Note

 Not all webhook events trigger workflows.

Like GitHub Actions workflows, agentic workflows can be triggered by repository events and schedules. For an example, see [Creating GitHub Agentic Workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/github-agentic-workflows/creating-github-agentic-workflows).

## `branch_protection_rule`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`branch_protection_rule`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#branch_protection_rule) | - `created` - `edited` - `deleted` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#branch_protection_rule). By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.

Runs your workflow when branch protection rules in the workflow repository are changed. For more information about branch protection rules, see [About protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches). For information about the branch protection rule APIs, see [Branches](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/branches#object-branchprotectionrule) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for branches and their settings](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/branches).

For example, you can run a workflow when a branch protection rule has been `created` or `deleted`:

```yaml
on:
  branch_protection_rule:
    types: [created, deleted]
```

## `check_run`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`check_run`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_run) | - `created` - `rerequested` - `completed` - `requested_action` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_run). By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- To prevent recursive workflows, this event does not trigger workflows if the check run's check suite was created by GitHub Actions or if the check suite's head SHA is associated with GitHub Actions.

Runs your workflow when activity related to a check run occurs. A check run is an individual test that is part of a check suite. For information, see [Using the REST API to interact with checks](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/using-the-rest-api-to-interact-with-checks). For information about the check run APIs, see [Checks](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/checks#object-checkrun) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for check runs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs).

For example, you can run a workflow when a check run has been `rerequested` or `completed`.

```yaml
on:
  check_run:
    types: [rerequested, completed]
```

## `check_suite`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`check_suite`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_suite) | - `completed` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_suite). Although only the `completed` activity type is supported, specifying the activity type will keep your workflow specific if more activity types are added in the future. By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- To prevent recursive workflows, this event does not trigger workflows if the check suite was created by GitHub Actions or if the check suite's head SHA is associated with GitHub Actions.

Runs your workflow when check suite activity occurs. A check suite is a collection of the check runs created for a specific commit. Check suites summarize the status and conclusion of the check runs that are in the suite. For information, see [Using the REST API to interact with checks](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/using-the-rest-api-to-interact-with-checks). For information about the check suite APIs, see [Checks](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/checks#object-checksuite) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for check suites](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/suites).

For example, you can run a workflow when a check suite has been `completed`.

```yaml
on:
  check_suite:
    types: [completed]
```

## `create`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`create`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#create) | Not applicable | Last commit on the created branch or tag | Branch or tag created |

Note

 An event will not be created when you create more than three tags at once.

Runs your workflow when someone creates a Git reference (Git branch or tag) in the workflow's repository. For information about the APIs to create a Git reference, see [Git](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/git#mutation-createref) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for Git references](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/refs#create-a-reference).

For example, you can run a workflow when the `create` event occurs.

```yaml
on:
  create
```

## `delete`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`delete`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#delete) | Not applicable | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- An event will not be created when you delete more than three tags at once.

blocks.text:
a conditional with the github.event.workflow_run.conclusion property. For example, this workflow will run whenever a workflow named "Build" completes, but the on-success job will only run if the "Build" workflow succeeded, and the on-failure job will only run if the "Build" workflow failed: 
 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Build ]
 types: [ completed ]

 jobs: 
 on-success: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' }} 
 steps: 
 - run: echo 'The triggering workflow passed' 
 on-failure: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'failure' }} 
 steps: 
 - run: echo 'The triggering workflow failed' 
 
 Limiting your workflow to run based on branches 
 You can use the branches or branches-ignore filter to specify what branches the triggering workflow must run on in order to trigger your workflow. For more information, see Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions . For example, a workflow with the following trigger will only run when the workflow named Build runs on a branch named canary . 
 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Build ]
 types: [ requested ]
 branches: [ canary ]
 
 Using data from the triggering workflow 
 You can access the workflow_run event payload that corresponds to the workflow that triggered your workflow. For example, if your triggering workflow generates artifacts, a workflow triggered with the workflow_run event can access these artifacts. 
 The following workflow uploads data as an artifact. (In this simplified example, the data is the pull request number.) 
 name: Upload data 

 on: 
 pull_request: 

 jobs: 
 upload: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 

 steps: 
 - name: Save PR number 
 env: 
 PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.number }} 
 run: |
 mkdir -p ./pr
 echo $PR_NUMBER > ./pr/pr_number
 - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 
 with: 
 name: pr_number 
 path: pr/ 
 
 When a run of the above workflow completes, it triggers a run of the following workflow. The following workflow uses the github.event.workflow_run context and the actions/download-artifact@v5 action to download the artifact that was uploaded by the above workflow, then comments on the pull request whose number was uploaded as an artifact. 
 name: Use the data 

 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Upload data ]
 types: 
 - completed 

 jobs: 
 download: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 permissions: 
 actions: read 
 issues: write 
 steps: 
 - name: 'Download artifact' 
 uses: actions/download-artifact@v5 
 with: 
 name: pr_number 
 # do not extract in the workspace dir that may contain executable scripts 
 path: ${{ runner.temp }}/artifacts 
 run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }} 
 github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} 

 - name: 'Comment on PR' 
 uses: actions/github-script@v8 
 with: 
 github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} 
 script: |
 const fs = require('fs');
 const path = require('path');
 const temp = '${{ runner.temp }}/artifacts';
 const issue_number_raw = fs.readFileSync(path.join(temp, 'pr_number'), 'utf8').trim();
 const issue_number = Number(issue_number_raw);
 if (!Number.isInteger(issue_number)) {
 throw new Error(`Invalid PR number in pr_number artifact: "${issue_number_raw}"`);
 }
 await github.rest.issues.createComment({
 owner: context.repo.owner,
 repo: context.repo.repo,
 issue_number: issue_number,
 body: 'Thank you for the PR!'
 });

{"content":"# gh-867 — RCA

## Root Cause Analysis

**Bug**: PRs merged by the Machine Merge Bot land on `main` but never trigger an 'Agent Pack Release' run — releases stall until an operator manually dispatches one (live 2026-10-11/12: #863 22:01Z, #866 00:11Z, both rescued by manual dispatch runs 38179243031 / 38188359001).

**Root cause**: `.github/workflows/agent-pack-release.yml` reacts to new commits on `main` ONLY through its `push` trigger. GitHub suppresses workflow triggers for events authored with `GITHUB_TOKEN` (documented: "events triggered by the GITHUB_TOKEN will not create a new workflow run"), and the merge bot's merge push lands with `GITHUB_TOKEN` — so the merge commit reaches `main` without any push event and the release workflow never learns about it. Human/operator merges (PAT/app-token pushes) fire normally — exactly the 21:14–21:18Z contrast pair in the ticket.

**Impact**: every machine-merged agent-code PR is invisible to the release pipeline. The SM fleet resolves agent packs via the 'latest' release knob, so machine-landed fixes never ship — tonight this twice stalled the fa #1457 fix pipeline until an operator noticed.

**Why the gh-844 kicker (previous mitigation) is insufficient**: the release kicker (`agent-pack-release-kicker.yml`, gh-844) is a 10-minute polling *belt*, not a trigger — it cannot meet the ~2-minute acceptance, and in both gh-867 incidents no release run appeared until a human dispatched one, i.e. the belt demonstrably did not rescue the machine-merge window either. The structural gap remains: nothing reacts *event-driven* to the machine merge completing.

**Fix approach** (ticket option 3): add a `workflow_run` trigger on 'Machine Merge Bot' completions to `agent-pack-release.yml`. The bot's own run completion is a normal GitHub event (workflow_run chains up to 3 levels are allowed — `Agent Docs → Machine Merge Bot → Agent Pack Release` is 2), so a machine merge now cuts a release within seconds. Two deliberate design points:
- **No `branches:` filter on the trigger** — the bot's `workflow_run.head_branch` is the *PR branch*, never `main`; a `branches: [main]` filter would silence the trigger entirely. "Filtered to main" is realized by the existing tag…main diff + `dist/.no-release` no-op (same dedup as the kicker's double-dispatch, gh-690).
- **Job gate on `conclusion == 'success'`** — the bot completes on every label latch tick (merging nothing) and `completed` covers failures; only a successful bot run may cut a release.
- The "Sync to current main" step (gh-690) is extended from push-only to push + workflow_run so a queued run releases current main; manual dispatch stays ref-targeted.
- Push trigger and kicker stay untouched (belt AND suspenders); the concurrency group + no-release no-op absorb double dispatches.

**Previous attempt**: gh-844 added the 10-minute release kicker after the 2026-10-10 #841 incident. It mitigates dropped push events generically but is polling-based: it misses the ~2-minute AC and, per both gh-867 incidents, did not rescue the machine-merge window (manual dispatch was still required).

## In this article

## Prerequisites

To learn more about workflows and triggering workflows, see [Workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/workflows).

## Triggering a workflow from a workflow

When you use the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` to perform tasks, events triggered by the `GITHUB_TOKEN` will not create a new workflow run, with the following exceptions:

- `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` events always create workflow runs.
- `pull_request` events with the `opened`, `synchronize`, or `reopened` activity types: when a workflow using `GITHUB_TOKEN` creates or updates a pull request, the resulting `pull_request` event creates workflow runs in an **approval-required** state. The pull request displays a banner in the merge box, and a user with write access to the repository can start the runs by selecting **Approve workflows to run**. Other `pull_request` activity types (such as `labeled`, `edited`, or `closed`) do not create workflow runs. This prevents recursive workflow runs while still allowing CI workflows to run on pull requests created by automation. For more information about approving workflow runs, see [Approving workflow runs from forks](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/approve-runs-from-forks).

For all other events, this behavior prevents you from accidentally creating recursive workflow runs. For example, if a workflow run pushes code using the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a new workflow will not run even when the repository contains a workflow configured to run when `push` events occur. For more information, see [Use GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication in workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/authenticate-with-github_token).

If you do want to trigger a workflow from within a workflow run, you can use a GitHub App installation access token or a personal access token instead of `GITHUB_TOKEN` to trigger events that require a token. Using one of these alternatives also lets `pull_request` workflows run automatically (without the approval prompt described above) when the pull request is created or updated by automation.

If you use a GitHub App, you'll need to create a GitHub App and store the app ID and private key as secrets. For more information, see [Making authenticated API requests with a GitHub App in a GitHub Actions workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/making-authenticated-api-requests-with-a-github-app-in-a-github-actions-workflow). If you use a personal access token, you'll need to create a personal access token and store it as a secret. For more information about creating a personal access token, see [Managing your personal access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens). For more information about storing secrets, see [Using secrets in GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets).

To minimize your GitHub Actions usage costs, ensure that you don't create recursive or unintended workflow runs.

For example, the following workflow uses a personal access token (stored as a secret called `MY_TOKEN`) to add a label to an issue via GitHub CLI. Any workflows that run when a label is added will run once this step is performed.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened

jobs:
  label_issue:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MY_TOKEN }}
          ISSUE_URL: ${{ github.event.issue.html_url }}
        run: |
          gh issue edit $ISSUE_URL --add-label "triage"
```

Conversely, the following workflow uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` to add a label to an issue. It will not trigger any workflows that run when a label is added.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened

jobs:
  label_issue:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          ISSUE_URL: ${{ github.event.issue.html_url }}
        run: |
          gh issue edit $ISSUE_URL --add-label "triage"
```

## Using events to trigger workflows

Use the `on` key to specify what events trigger your workflow. For more information about events you can use, see [Events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows).

### Using a single event

For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when a push is made to any branch in the workflow's repository:

```yaml
on: push
```

### Using multiple events

You can specify a single event or multiple events. For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when a push is made to any branch in the repository or when someone forks the repository:

```yaml
on: [push, fork]
```

If you specify multiple events, only one of those events needs to occur to trigger your workflow. If multiple triggering events for your workflow occur at the same time, multiple workflow runs will be triggered.

### Using activity types and filters with multiple events

You can use activity types and filters to further control when your workflow will run. For more information, see Using event activity types and Using filters. If you specify activity types or filters for an event and your workflow triggers on multiple events, you must configure each event separately. You must append a colon (`:`) to all events, including events without configuration.

For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when:

- A label is created
- A push is made to the `main` branch in the repository
- A push is made to a GitHub Pages-enabled branch

```yaml
on:
  label:
    types:
      - created
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  page_build:
```

## Using event activity types

Some events have activity types that give you more control over when your workflow should run. Use `on.<event_name>.types` to define the type of event activity that will trigger a workflow run.

For example, the `issue_comment` event has the `created`, `edited`, and `deleted` activity types. If your workflow triggers on the `label` event, it will run whenever a label is created, edited, or deleted. If you specify the `created` activity type for the `label` event, your workflow will run when a label is created but not when a label is edited or deleted.

```yaml
on:
  label:
    types:
      - created
```

If you specify multiple activity types, only one of those event activity types needs to occur to trigger your workflow. If multiple triggering event activity types for your workflow occur at the same time, multiple workflow runs will be triggered. For example, the following workflow triggers when an issue is opened or labeled. If an issue with two labels is opened, three workflow runs will start: one for the issue opened event and two for the two issue labeled events.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened
      - labeled
```

For more information about each event and their activity types, see [Events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows).

## Using filters

Some events have filters that give you more control over when your workflow should run.

For example, the `push` event has a `branches` filter that causes your workflow to run only when a push to a branch that matches the `branches` filter occurs, instead of when any push occurs.

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
      - 'releases/**'
```

### Using filters to target specific branches for pull request events

When using the `pull_request` and `pull_request_target` events, you can configure a workflow to run only for pull requests that target specific branches.

# Events that trigger workflows

You can configure your workflows to run when specific activity on GitHub happens, at a scheduled time, or when an event outside of GitHub occurs.

Copy markdown

## In this article

## About events that trigger workflows

Workflow triggers are events that cause a workflow to run. For more information about how to use workflow triggers, see [Triggering a workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-when-workflows-run/trigger-a-workflow).

Some events have multiple activity types. For these events, you can specify which activity types will trigger a workflow run. For more information about what each activity type means, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads).

Note

 Not all webhook events trigger workflows.

Like GitHub Actions workflows, agentic workflows can be triggered by repository events and schedules. For an example, see [Creating GitHub Agentic Workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/copilot/how-tos/github-agentic-workflows/creating-github-agentic-workflows).

## `branch_protection_rule`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`branch_protection_rule`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#branch_protection_rule) | - `created` - `edited` - `deleted` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#branch_protection_rule). By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.

Runs your workflow when branch protection rules in the workflow repository are changed. For more information about branch protection rules, see [About protected branches](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches). For information about the branch protection rule APIs, see [Branches](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/branches#object-branchprotectionrule) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for branches and their settings](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/branches).

For example, you can run a workflow when a branch protection rule has been `created` or `deleted`:

```yaml
on:
  branch_protection_rule:
    types: [created, deleted]
```

## `check_run`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`check_run`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_run) | - `created` - `rerequested` - `completed` - `requested_action` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_run). By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- To prevent recursive workflows, this event does not trigger workflows if the check run's check suite was created by GitHub Actions or if the check suite's head SHA is associated with GitHub Actions.

Runs your workflow when activity related to a check run occurs. A check run is an individual test that is part of a check suite. For information, see [Using the REST API to interact with checks](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/using-the-rest-api-to-interact-with-checks). For information about the check run APIs, see [Checks](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/checks#object-checkrun) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for check runs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs).

For example, you can run a workflow when a check run has been `rerequested` or `completed`.

```yaml
on:
  check_run:
    types: [rerequested, completed]
```

## `check_suite`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`check_suite`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_suite) | - `completed` | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- More than one activity type triggers this event. For information about each activity type, see [Webhook events and payloads](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#check_suite). Although only the `completed` activity type is supported, specifying the activity type will keep your workflow specific if more activity types are added in the future. By default, all activity types trigger workflows that run on this event. You can limit your workflow runs to specific activity types using the `types` keyword. For more information, see [Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/workflow-syntax#onevent_nametypes).
- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- To prevent recursive workflows, this event does not trigger workflows if the check suite was created by GitHub Actions or if the check suite's head SHA is associated with GitHub Actions.

Runs your workflow when check suite activity occurs. A check suite is a collection of the check runs created for a specific commit. Check suites summarize the status and conclusion of the check runs that are in the suite. For information, see [Using the REST API to interact with checks](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/guides/using-the-rest-api-to-interact-with-checks). For information about the check suite APIs, see [Checks](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/checks#object-checksuite) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for check suites](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/suites).

For example, you can run a workflow when a check suite has been `completed`.

```yaml
on:
  check_suite:
    types: [completed]
```

## `create`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`create`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#create) | Not applicable | Last commit on the created branch or tag | Branch or tag created |

Note

 An event will not be created when you create more than three tags at once.

Runs your workflow when someone creates a Git reference (Git branch or tag) in the workflow's repository. For information about the APIs to create a Git reference, see [Git](https://docs.github.com/en/graphql/reference/git#mutation-createref) in the GraphQL API documentation or [REST API endpoints for Git references](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/refs#create-a-reference).

For example, you can run a workflow when the `create` event occurs.

```yaml
on:
  create
```

## `delete`

| Webhook event payload | Activity types | `GITHUB_SHA` | `GITHUB_REF` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [`delete`](https://docs.github.com/en/webhooks/webhook-events-and-payloads#delete) | Not applicable | Last commit on default branch | Default branch |

Note

- This event will only trigger a workflow run if the workflow file exists on the default branch.
- An event will not be created when you delete more than three tags at once.

blocks.text:
a conditional with the github.event.workflow_run.conclusion property. For example, this workflow will run whenever a workflow named "Build" completes, but the on-success job will only run if the "Build" workflow succeeded, and the on-failure job will only run if the "Build" workflow failed: 
 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Build ]
 types: [ completed ]

 jobs: 
 on-success: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' }} 
 steps: 
 - run: echo 'The triggering workflow passed' 
 on-failure: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 if: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'failure' }} 
 steps: 
 - run: echo 'The triggering workflow failed' 
 
 Limiting your workflow to run based on branches 
 You can use the branches or branches-ignore filter to specify what branches the triggering workflow must run on in order to trigger your workflow. For more information, see Workflow syntax for GitHub Actions . For example, a workflow with the following trigger will only run when the workflow named Build runs on a branch named canary . 
 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Build ]
 types: [ requested ]
 branches: [ canary ]
 
 Using data from the triggering workflow 
 You can access the workflow_run event payload that corresponds to the workflow that triggered your workflow. For example, if your triggering workflow generates artifacts, a workflow triggered with the workflow_run event can access these artifacts. 
 The following workflow uploads data as an artifact. (In this simplified example, the data is the pull request number.) 
 name: Upload data 

 on: 
 pull_request: 

 jobs: 
 upload: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 

 steps: 
 - name: Save PR number 
 env: 
 PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.number }} 
 run: |
 mkdir -p ./pr
 echo $PR_NUMBER > ./pr/pr_number
 - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 
 with: 
 name: pr_number 
 path: pr/ 
 
 When a run of the above workflow completes, it triggers a run of the following workflow. The following workflow uses the github.event.workflow_run context and the actions/download-artifact@v5 action to download the artifact that was uploaded by the above workflow, then comments on the pull request whose number was uploaded as an artifact. 
 name: Use the data 

 on: 
 workflow_run: 
 workflows: [ Upload data ]
 types: 
 - completed 

 jobs: 
 download: 
 runs-on: ubuntu-latest 
 permissions: 
 actions: read 
 issues: write 
 steps: 
 - name: 'Download artifact' 
 uses: actions/download-artifact@v5 
 with: 
 name: pr_number 
 # do not extract in the workspace dir that may contain executable scripts 
 path: ${{ runner.temp }}/artifacts 
 run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }} 
 github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} 

 - name: 'Comment on PR' 
 uses: actions/github-script@v8 
 with: 
 github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} 
 script: |
 const fs = require('fs');
 const path = require('path');
 const temp = '${{ runner.temp }}/artifacts';
 const issue_number_raw = fs.readFileSync(path.join(temp, 'pr_number'), 'utf8').trim();
 const issue_number = Number(issue_number_raw);
 if (!Number.isInteger(issue_number)) {
 throw new Error(`Invalid PR number in pr_number artifact: "${issue_number_raw}"`);
 }
 await github.rest.issues.createComment({
 owner: context.repo.owner,
 repo: context.repo.repo,
 issue_number: issue_number,
 body: 'Thank you for the PR!'
 });

{"content":"# gh-867 — RCA

## Root Cause Analysis

**Bug**: PRs merged by the Machine Merge Bot land on `main` but never trigger an 'Agent Pack Release' run — releases stall until an operator manually dispatches one (live 2026-10-11/12: #863 22:01Z, #866 00:11Z, both rescued by manual dispatch runs 38179243031 / 38188359001).

**Root cause**: `.github/workflows/agent-pack-release.yml` reacts to new commits on `main` ONLY through its `push` trigger. GitHub suppresses workflow triggers for events authored with `GITHUB_TOKEN` (documented: "events triggered by the GITHUB_TOKEN will not create a new workflow run"), and the merge bot's merge push lands with `GITHUB_TOKEN` — so the merge commit reaches `main` without any push event and the release workflow never learns about it. Human/operator merges (PAT/app-token pushes) fire normally — exactly the 21:14–21:18Z contrast pair in the ticket.

**Impact**: every machine-merged agent-code PR is invisible to the release pipeline. The SM fleet resolves agent packs via the 'latest' release knob, so machine-landed fixes never ship — tonight this twice stalled the fa #1457 fix pipeline until an operator noticed.

**Why the gh-844 kicker (previous mitigation) is insufficient**: the release kicker (`agent-pack-release-kicker.yml`, gh-844) is a 10-minute polling *belt*, not a trigger — it cannot meet the ~2-minute acceptance, and in both gh-867 incidents no release run appeared until a human dispatched one, i.e. the belt demonstrably did not rescue the machine-merge window either. The structural gap remains: nothing reacts *event-driven* to the machine merge completing.

**Fix approach** (ticket option 3): add a `workflow_run` trigger on 'Machine Merge Bot' completions to `agent-pack-release.yml`. The bot's own run completion is a normal GitHub event (workflow_run chains up to 3 levels are allowed — `Agent Docs → Machine Merge Bot → Agent Pack Release` is 2), so a machine merge now cuts a release within seconds. Two deliberate design points:
- **No `branches:` filter on the trigger** — the bot's `workflow_run.head_branch` is the *PR branch*, never `main`; a `branches: [main]` filter would silence the trigger entirely. "Filtered to main" is realized by the existing tag…main diff + `dist/.no-release` no-op (same dedup as the kicker's double-dispatch, gh-690).
- **Job gate on `conclusion == 'success'`** — the bot completes on every label latch tick (merging nothing) and `completed` covers failures; only a successful bot run may cut a release.
- The "Sync to current main" step (gh-690) is extended from push-only to push + workflow_run so a queued run releases current main; manual dispatch stays ref-targeted.
- Push trigger and kicker stay untouched (belt AND suspenders); the concurrency group + no-release no-op absorb double dispatches.

**Previous attempt**: gh-844 added the 10-minute release kicker after the 2026-10-10 #841 incident. It mitigates dropped push events generically but is polling-based: it misses the ~2-minute AC and, per both gh-867 incidents, did not rescue the machine-merge window (manual dispatch was still required).

# Triggering a workflow

How to automatically trigger GitHub Actions workflows

Copy markdown

## In this article

## Prerequisites

To learn more about workflows and triggering workflows, see [Workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/workflows).

## Triggering a workflow from a workflow

When you use the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN` to perform tasks, events triggered by the `GITHUB_TOKEN` will not create a new workflow run, with the following exceptions:

- `workflow_dispatch` and `repository_dispatch` events always create workflow runs.
- `pull_request` events with the `opened`, `synchronize`, or `reopened` activity types: when a workflow using `GITHUB_TOKEN` creates or updates a pull request, the resulting `pull_request` event creates workflow runs in an **approval-required** state. The pull request displays a banner in the merge box, and a user with write access to the repository can start the runs by selecting **Approve workflows to run**. Other `pull_request` activity types (such as `labeled`, `edited`, or `closed`) do not create workflow runs. This prevents recursive workflow runs while still allowing CI workflows to run on pull requests created by automation. For more information about approving workflow runs, see [Approving workflow runs from forks](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/manage-workflow-runs/approve-runs-from-forks).

For all other events, this behavior prevents you from accidentally creating recursive workflow runs. For example, if a workflow run pushes code using the repository's `GITHUB_TOKEN`, a new workflow will not run even when the repository contains a workflow configured to run when `push` events occur. For more information, see [Use GITHUB_TOKEN for authentication in workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/authenticate-with-github_token).

If you do want to trigger a workflow from within a workflow run, you can use a GitHub App installation access token or a personal access token instead of `GITHUB_TOKEN` to trigger events that require a token. Using one of these alternatives also lets `pull_request` workflows run automatically (without the approval prompt described above) when the pull request is created or updated by automation.

If you use a GitHub App, you'll need to create a GitHub App and store the app ID and private key as secrets. For more information, see [Making authenticated API requests with a GitHub App in a GitHub Actions workflow](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/making-authenticated-api-requests-with-a-github-app-in-a-github-actions-workflow). If you use a personal access token, you'll need to create a personal access token and store it as a secret. For more information about creating a personal access token, see [Managing your personal access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/keeping-your-account-and-data-secure/managing-your-personal-access-tokens). For more information about storing secrets, see [Using secrets in GitHub Actions](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/write-workflows/choose-what-workflows-do/use-secrets).

To minimize your GitHub Actions usage costs, ensure that you don't create recursive or unintended workflow runs.

For example, the following workflow uses a personal access token (stored as a secret called `MY_TOKEN`) to add a label to an issue via GitHub CLI. Any workflows that run when a label is added will run once this step is performed.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened

jobs:
  label_issue:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.MY_TOKEN }}
          ISSUE_URL: ${{ github.event.issue.html_url }}
        run: |
          gh issue edit $ISSUE_URL --add-label "triage"
```

Conversely, the following workflow uses `GITHUB_TOKEN` to add a label to an issue. It will not trigger any workflows that run when a label is added.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened

jobs:
  label_issue:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - env:
          GH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
          ISSUE_URL: ${{ github.event.issue.html_url }}
        run: |
          gh issue edit $ISSUE_URL --add-label "triage"
```

## Using events to trigger workflows

Use the `on` key to specify what events trigger your workflow. For more information about events you can use, see [Events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows).

### Using a single event

For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when a push is made to any branch in the workflow's repository:

```yaml
on: push
```

### Using multiple events

You can specify a single event or multiple events. For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when a push is made to any branch in the repository or when someone forks the repository:

```yaml
on: [push, fork]
```

If you specify multiple events, only one of those events needs to occur to trigger your workflow. If multiple triggering events for your workflow occur at the same time, multiple workflow runs will be triggered.

### Using activity types and filters with multiple events

You can use activity types and filters to further control when your workflow will run. For more information, see Using event activity types and Using filters. If you specify activity types or filters for an event and your workflow triggers on multiple events, you must configure each event separately. You must append a colon (`:`) to all events, including events without configuration.

For example, a workflow with the following `on` value will run when:

- A label is created
- A push is made to the `main` branch in the repository
- A push is made to a GitHub Pages-enabled branch

```yaml
on:
  label:
    types:
      - created
  push:
    branches:
      - main
  page_build:
```

## Using event activity types

Some events have activity types that give you more control over when your workflow should run. Use `on.<event_name>.types` to define the type of event activity that will trigger a workflow run.

For example, the `issue_comment` event has the `created`, `edited`, and `deleted` activity types. If your workflow triggers on the `label` event, it will run whenever a label is created, edited, or deleted. If you specify the `created` activity type for the `label` event, your workflow will run when a label is created but not when a label is edited or deleted.

```yaml
on:
  label:
    types:
      - created
```

If you specify multiple activity types, only one of those event activity types needs to occur to trigger your workflow. If multiple triggering event activity types for your workflow occur at the same time, multiple workflow runs will be triggered. For example, the following workflow triggers when an issue is opened or labeled. If an issue with two labels is opened, three workflow runs will start: one for the issue opened event and two for the two issue labeled events.

```yaml
on:
  issues:
    types:
      - opened
      - labeled
```

For more information about each event and their activity types, see [Events that trigger workflows](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows).

## Using filters

Some events have filters that give you more control over when your workflow should run.

For example, the `push` event has a `branches` filter that causes your workflow to run only when a push to a branch that matches the `branches` filter occurs, instead of when any push occurs.

```yaml
on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main
      - 'releases/**'
```

### Using filters to target specific branches for pull request events

When using the `pull_request` and `pull_request_target` events, you can configure a workflow to run only for pull requests that target specific branches.

Use the `branches` filter when you want to include branch name patterns or when you want to both include and excl…
